## Privacy Law Always Chases Technology {.center}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
> The law must provide some relief to individuals when the acts of others
> interfere with their **right to be let alone.**
> — Warren & Brandeis, *The Right to Privacy*, 1890

A new technology arrives, a harm becomes visible, and the law reacts. That
pattern repeats from gossip photography to mainframes to AI.
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.legacy}
<!-- from ppt-archive/11-PrivacyLaw.pptx slide 2 -->
![](images/slide002_img002.png){height="430px"}
:::
::: {.caption}
*Harvard Law Review*, Dec. 15, 1890: the article that invented the privacy tort.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Warren and Brandeis wrote "The Right to Privacy" for the Harvard Law Review in
1890 in response to a new technology — instantaneous photography — and to
gossip journalism. Warren was reportedly enraged by Boston newspapers covering
his family's social events. The article invented the U.S. right-to-privacy
tort. The whole lecture is organized around this reactive pattern: name the
technology, name the harm, name the law that followed. Cold-call: what's the
2026 version of gossip photography? Model training on scraped data,
age-verification wallets, and always-on ACR on smart TVs are the ones I'd
prime the room to consider. Hold this pattern as the deck's spine — every
statute later in the deck is another instance of it.
:::

VPPA in about a year) and then ask the room to fill in a fifth row for 2026:
model training on scraped data, age-verification wallets, always-on smart-TV
recognition. The last row is deliberately not a new statute: it is old law
stretched over a new technology, which is the U.S. story from here on.
:::


## A 2026 Hook: The FTC Still Sets the Floor {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.vignette}
**Dec. 31, 2025:** a federal court approved a **$10M** order against **Disney**
for letting children's data be collected through mislabeled "Made for Kids"
YouTube videos, a **COPPA** violation
([FTC, Dec. 2025](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2025/12/court-approves-order-requiring-disney-pay-10-million-settle-ftc-allegations-firm-enabled-unlawful)).
:::

**May 4, 2026:** the FTC settled with **Kochava**, banning sale of *sensitive*
location data (medical, religious, shelters, schools) without express consent
([FTC, May 2026](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/05/ftc-ban-kochava-subsidiary-selling-sensitive-location-data-settle-charges-they-sold-location-data)).

Old statutes, new harms.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 5.6
//| fig-height: 4.6
digraph floor {
  rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.3; ranksep=0.45;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=19, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.18,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=17];
bgcolor="transparent";

  none [label="No comprehensive federal\nprivacy law", fillcolor="#f8d7c4", penwidth=2];
  coppa [label="COPPA (1998)\nchildren under 13", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  s5 [label="FTC Act Section 5 (1914)\nunfair or deceptive practices", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  d [label="Disney, $10M\n(Dec. 2025)", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
  k [label="Kochava: sensitive location\ndata ban (May 2026)", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
  none -> coppa [label="so the regulator reaches for"]; none -> s5;
  coppa -> d; s5 -> k;
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the freshest concrete anchor for the deck. Two teaching points to
land. First: the regulator is reaching for a narrow 1998 tool (COPPA) and a
general 1914 consumer-protection statute (Section 5) because there is nothing
comprehensive. Disney allegedly failed to label some YouTube uploads "Made
for Kids" — the designation Google agreed to in the 2019 YouTube COPPA
settlement — enabling targeted ads to under-13s. Second: enforcement is real
and current, not historical. Kochava is the more legally interesting anchor
because it rests on the unfairness prong of Section 5 (no broken promise
required) after nearly four years of litigation. Both anchors make the same
teaching point: no federal statute means a 1998 kids' law and a 1914
consumer-protection statute do the work. Swap in whatever broke this week —
the FTC press feed always has something.
:::

# Where Modern Privacy Law Comes From {.center}

FIPPs → PII → the U.S. patchwork → the FTC → GDPR

## Computerized Records Created New Threats {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
By the 1970s, mainframes made four things newly possible:

- **Unknown databases** holding information about you
- **Cheap mass collection**: scale flips the cost-benefit of surveillance
- **One-to-many dissemination** of records
- **Linking** information gathered different ways
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 6.8
//| fig-height: 4.6
digraph threats {
  rankdir=LR; nodesep=0.18; ranksep=0.55;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=18, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.18,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=16];
bgcolor="transparent";

  bank [label="Bank", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; emp [label="Employer", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  hosp [label="Hospital", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; gov [label="Agency", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; school [label="School", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  db [label="Database you\ndo not know exists", fillcolor="#f8d7c4", penwidth=2];
  link [label="Linked on name,\nSSN, address", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"];
  dossier [label="One dossier", fillcolor="#f2d9a8"];
  out1 [label="Lender", fillcolor="#d9efd3"]; out2 [label="Employer", fillcolor="#d9efd3"]; out3 [label="Police", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
  bank -> db; emp -> db; hosp -> db; gov -> db; school -> db;
  db -> link -> dossier; dossier -> out1; dossier -> out2; dossier -> out3;
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Standard historical anchor. These 1970s concerns sound quaint until you note
that every one is roughly a hundred times worse with cloud, smartphones, and
ad-tech. The four threats — unknown databases, mass collection, dissemination,
linkage — are the same four Latanya Sweeney would empirically confirm with
re-identification attacks two decades later, and the same four the AOL search
log leak of 2006 realized in miniature. The point: the structure of the
threat — scale, linkage, opacity — is what the law tried to address, and it's
the same structure today. If a student pushes back that these worries are
overblown, forward-reference the Sweeney and Netflix Prize slides.
:::

## FIPPs: The Foundation (HEW, 1973) {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
The HEW report *Records, Computers, and the Rights of Citizens* gave us the
**Fair Information Practice Principles**:

1. **No secret** record-keeping systems
2. A way to **know** what is collected and how it is used
3. A way to **prevent secondary use** without consent
4. A way to **correct** your record
5. **Reasonable security** and reliability for intended use

Almost every privacy law worldwide descends from these five ideas.
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.legacy}
<!-- from ppt-archive/11-PrivacyLaw.pptx slides 4 and 6 -->
![](images/slide004_img004.png){height="330px"}

![](images/slide006_img007.png){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.caption}
The 1973 report and its transmittal letter: "a framework for recordkeeping about people."
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Primary source is HEW's 1973 report "Records, Computers, and the Rights of
Citizens" — every modern regime descends from these five principles: the OECD
1980 guidelines, the EU 1995 Data Protection Directive, GDPR, and CCPA. Tell
students to memorize the five FIPPs; when we hit GDPR two segments from now,
they will see the same DNA — notice, access/rectification, purpose limitation,
security — mapped cleanly onto GDPR Articles 5 and 12–22. Emphasize the
through-line: transparency, control, correction, and security. The open
question for the rest of the lecture: does this 1973 model still fit a world
of inference and machine learning? That's the setup for the "Age of
Inference" slide three slides from now.
:::

## The FIPPs in Practice: the Default Decides {.smaller}

**Notice** · **appropriate use** (primary vs. secondary) · **individual choice** (opt-in vs. opt-out) · **access and correction** · **security** · **minimization**

![](images/consent-defaults.svg){width="88%" fig-align="center"}

::: {.caption}
Effective consent to organ donation by national default (Johnson & Goldstein, *Science* 2003). Same question, opposite default, opposite answer. The U.S. privacy default is opt-out; GDPR's is opt-in.
:::

::: {.notes}
Opt-in versus opt-out is the sleeper concept — it looks technical but drives
everything downstream. The canonical empirical result is Johnson and Goldstein,
"Do Defaults Save Lives?", Science 302:1338, 2003 — default-opt-in produces
roughly 90%+ compliance, default-opt-out produces under 5%. GDPR is opt-in
for most processing; the U.S. defaults to opt-out, and the empirical fact is
that almost no one ever opts out. That single design choice determines whether
a "choice" regime protects anyone. Cookie banners, breach-notification
opt-outs, GDPR consent, CCPA opt-out — one design switch, huge downstream
effect. Foreshadows the Meeting 12 dark-patterns research.
:::

## Notice and Consent Is Broken {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
The model assumes a person reads, understands, and meaningfully agrees.

- Policies run **thousands of words** and change without warning
- Stated policy and actual practice **diverge**; that gap is what the FTC sues on
- "Consent" via a cookie wall is not a real choice

Reading every policy you encounter would take about **244 hours a year** (McDonald & Cranor, 2008).
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.capture}
[![](images/captures/tosdr-instagram.png){width="100%"}](https://tosdr.org/en/service/219)

ToS;DR grades Instagram's terms "E". Live site, captured Nov 11 2026; click to open.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the central critique of the orthodox model. Canonical reading:
Aleecia McDonald and Lorrie Cranor, "The Cost of Reading Privacy Policies,"
I/S: A Journal of Law and Policy, 2008 — they estimated 244 hours per year
per person to read the policies of the sites they visit. The definitive
academic critique is Solove's "Privacy Self-Management and the Consent
Dilemma," 126 Harvard Law Review 1880 (2013) — putting the burden on the
individual doesn't work because the individual has neither the time nor the
information to bear it. Live demo if time: ToS;DR grades real privacy
policies. Connect forward: the FTC's deception theory exists precisely
because the gap between promise and practice is where the harm lives.
:::

## The Model FIPPs Assumed: Records and Joins {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
<!-- recovered from ppt-archive/11-PrivacyLaw.pptx slide 17 -->
![](images/records-join-model.png){width="100%"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
- A computer **stores** a record and hands it back later
- Each field **means what it says** — a name is a name, a ZIP is a ZIP
- The only "processing" is a **join**: match two records on an ID
- So FIPPs guard the **record** — notice, access, correction, security
:::
:::

This is the 1973 picture of computing. The next slide asks what breaks when
it stops being true.

::: {.notes}
Static figure recovered from the original deck; walk it left to right. Two
tables, each keyed by an ID — one holds some data about you, the other holds
more. The arrows are the only operation the 1970s model imagined: a join on
the key, producing one wider record. Three assumptions ride along. The data
sits still until someone retrieves it. Its meaning is evident on its face —
no interpretation needed. And the harm model is linkage: if a bad actor can
join these two rows, they learn more than either row revealed. Every FIPP
makes sense against this picture — notice tells you a row exists, access
lets you read it, correction fixes a wrong field, security locks the table.
Then point to the next slide: today's systems query, infer, and generate
conclusions you never wrote down anywhere, and the join is the least of it.
:::


## Re-Examining FIPPs in the Age of Inference {.smaller}

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 12
//| fig-height: 3.3
digraph infer {
  rankdir=LR; nodesep=0.25; ranksep=0.5;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=19, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.18,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=17];
bgcolor="transparent";

  subgraph cluster_old { label="The 1973 model: records"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=21; color="#bbbbbb"; style="rounded";
    o1 [label="Collect", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; o2 [label="Store", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; o3 [label="Retrieve or join", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; o4 [label="Act on what\nyou disclosed", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
    o1 -> o2 -> o3 -> o4; }
  subgraph cluster_new { label="Today: inference"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=21; color="#bbbbbb"; style="rounded";
    n1 [label="Collect\n(and query, not ship)", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; n2 [label="Train a model", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; n3 [label="Infer facts you\nnever disclosed", fillcolor="#f8d7c4", penwidth=2]; n4 [label="Act on the\ninference", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
    n1 -> n2 -> n3 -> n4; }
}
```

- FIPPs guard the **record**: notice, access, correction, security. Inference produces conclusions that were never in any record (a retailer inferring a pregnancy from purchases).
- **Differential privacy** deliberately adds **noise**: it violates "data must be correct," yet *enhances* privacy. Some FIPPs now point the wrong way.

::: {.notes}
This is the most intellectually interesting slide in the deck. FIPPs were
built for static records; modern systems infer. The canonical example is
Kashmir Hill's February 2012 Forbes piece on Target inferring a teenager's
pregnancy from purchase patterns — no PII was leaked, yet a deeply private
fact was produced and mailed to the family home. On differential privacy,
the readable intro is Chapter 1 of Dwork and Roth, "The Algorithmic
Foundations of Differential Privacy," 2014 — noise is the privacy, which
directly contradicts the FIPPs accuracy principle. That's the paradox: some
FIPPs (accuracy, minimization-of-error) point the opposite direction from
what actually protects privacy today. Ask: does the 1973 model even name the
harm from inference? Debate hook — should we replace FIPPs, patch them, or
build a parallel framework for inferential harms?
:::

## PII Is Not a Bright Line {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
The classic assumption: scrub name, SSN, address, and the data is "safe."

**Wrong.** Any combination of attributes that singles out one person re-identifies them.

- **AOL (2006):** "anonymized" search logs re-identified by *The New York Times*
- **Netflix Prize (2006):** ratings re-identified by Narayanan & Shmatikov
- **Massachusetts health records:** Sweeney re-identified the governor via ZIP + birth date + sex

So is **ZIP code** PII? Is an **IP address**? The line dissolves under inference.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 6.4
//| fig-height: 4.6
digraph sweeney {
  rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.5; ranksep=0.5;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=18, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.18,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=17];
bgcolor="transparent";

  med [label="Hospital discharge data\n(sold as \"anonymized\")\nZIP · birth date · sex\ndiagnosis · procedures", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  vote [label="Voter list ($20)\nname · address · party\nZIP · birth date · sex", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  key [label="ZIP + birth date + sex\nunique for 87% of Americans", fillcolor="#f8d7c4", penwidth=2];
  out [label="Name + diagnosis", fillcolor="#f2d9a8", penwidth=2];
  med -> key; vote -> key; key -> out;
}
```
::: {.caption}
Sweeney (2000). Today 15 attributes re-identify 99.98% of Americans (Rocher et al., 2019).
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
PII is a legal fiction that engineering keeps breaking. The three re-id
results are the canon. AOL, August 2006: Barbaro and Zeller of the New York
Times identified "AOL Searcher No. 4417749" as Thelma Arnold, a 62-year-old
Georgia widow, from her supposedly-anonymized search log. Netflix Prize:
Narayanan and Shmatikov, "Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets,"
IEEE S&P 2008. Sweeney: her 2000 paper "Simple Demographics Often Identify
People Uniquely" showed 87% of U.S. residents were uniquely identified by
ZIP plus date-of-birth plus sex. Modern update — Rocher, Hendrickx, and de
Montjoye, Nature Communications 2019 — 15 attributes suffice for over 99.98%
of Americans. Make students articulate why removing identifiers fails:
quasi-identifiers in combination are uniquely identifying. Modern laws have
shifted from "remove PII" to "reasonably cannot be linked" standards (e.g.,
CCPA de-identification) — and even that is hard to define.
:::

# The U.S. Patchwork {.center}

Sectoral, reactive, incomplete, by design

## Sectoral vs. Omnibus {.smaller}

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 12.4
//| fig-height: 4.2
digraph sect {
  rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.18; ranksep=0.4;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=18, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.16,0.07"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=16];
bgcolor="transparent";
  subgraph cluster_us { label="United States: one law per sector, per harm, per actor"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=21; color="#bbbbbb"; style="rounded";
    u1 [label="Health providers\nHIPAA", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; u2 [label="Credit bureaus\nFCRA", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; u3 [label="Children\nCOPPA", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
    u4 [label="Schools\nFERPA", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; u5 [label="Banks\nGLBA", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; u6 [label="Video rentals\nVPPA", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
    g1 [label="Fitness and\nperiod apps", style="dashed,rounded", fillcolor="#ffffff", fontcolor="#a00000"]; g2 [label="Data brokers", style="dashed,rounded", fillcolor="#ffffff", fontcolor="#a00000"];
    g3 [label="Ad-tech", style="dashed,rounded", fillcolor="#ffffff", fontcolor="#a00000"]; g4 [label="Smart TVs,\nvoice assistants", style="dashed,rounded", fillcolor="#ffffff", fontcolor="#a00000"];
    gap [label="The gaps: FTC Section 5 or nothing", fillcolor="#f8d7c4", penwidth=2];
    u1 -> g1 [style=invis]; u2 -> g2 [style=invis]; u3 -> g3 [style=invis]; u4 -> g4 [style=invis];
    g1 -> gap; g2 -> gap; g3 -> gap; g4 -> gap; }
  subgraph cluster_eu { label="European Union: one law"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=21; color="#bbbbbb"; style="rounded";
    eu [label="GDPR\nall personal data, any sector,\nany organization that touches\nan EU resident", fillcolor="#d9efd3", penwidth=2]; }
}
```

Rights attach to the **industry** in the U.S. and to the **data** in the EU. This one distinction explains most U.S./EU differences in the lecture.

::: {.notes}
Burn this dichotomy in — it's a midterm staple. Sectoral means coverage has
holes by construction (every gap is a lawsuit or an FTC case). Omnibus means
one rulebook but heavy compliance and often uneven enforcement. Neither is
obviously right — that's the GDPR debate at the end of the deck, and the
Omnibus breakout later this week. Best-of-both defenders point to Illinois
BIPA (a sectoral state law with a private right of action, which produced a
$650M Facebook settlement) as evidence that sectoral can be sharp when it
wants to be. The private right of action is the sleeper design feature that
turns sectoral law from paper into teeth.
:::

## The Patchwork, Statute by Statute {.smaller}

![](images/statute-timeline.svg){width="100%"}

Each statute fights the last scandal and stops at its boundary: **who holds the data** (FCRA, Privacy Act), **a specific anecdote** (VPPA, DPPA), **a data-sharing deal** (HIPAA, GLBA), or **a special category** (COPPA, GINA). The dates are not a plan; Congress reacted issue by issue.

::: {.notes}
The VPPA story is the keeper — and the perfect illustration of the pattern.
In September 1987 Michael Dolan published "The Bork Tapes" in the Washington
City Paper, listing Judge Robert Bork's video rentals during his Supreme
Court nomination. Congress passed the Video Privacy Protection Act,
18 U.S.C. § 2710, in October 1988 — roughly a year later — but only about
video tapes. That's sectoral lawmaking in a nutshell: each statute fights
the last scandal and stops at the boundary of that scandal. The FCRA/FERPA/
HIPAA/GLBA/COPPA/GINA statute list is the canonical "sectoral by anecdote"
survey. Cold-call: what would the equivalent modern statute be — a
"Streaming Video Privacy Act"? A "Voice Assistant Privacy Act"? Note the
dates aren't chronological because Congress reacted issue by issue.
:::

## The HIPAA Gap {.smaller}

HIPAA covers **covered entities** (providers, plans, clearinghouses) and their vendors, not "health data" as such.

```{dot}
//| fig-height: 4

  rankdir=TB; nodesep=0.22; ranksep=0.35;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=18, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.16,0.07"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=16];
bgcolor="transparent";

  subgraph cluster_out { label="Outside HIPAA: the health data you actually generate"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=20; color="#a00000"; style="rounded,dashed";
    a1 [label="Fitness apps", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; a2 [label="Period trackers", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; a3 [label="Mental-health apps", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; a4 [label="Consumer DNA kits", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; a5 [label="Pharmacy discount apps", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; }
  s5 [label="Only FTC Section 5 reaches here", fillcolor="#f2d9a8", penwidth=2];
  p -> a1 [style=invis]; h -> a2 [style=invis]; c -> a3 [style=invis]; ba -> a4 [style=invis];
  a1 -> s5; a2 -> s5; a3 -> s5; a4 -> s5; a5 -> s5;
}
```

- **GoodRx**, $1.5M (2023), shared health data for ads; **BetterHelp**, $7.8M (2023), shared mental-health data with Facebook. Both reached by **FTC Section 5**, because HIPAA could not.

::: {.notes}
This is the single most useful slide for showing why sectoral law fails.
The key teaching move: HIPAA regulates covered entities — providers, plans,
clearinghouses, and their business associates — not "health data as such."
Consumer apps, wearables, period trackers, 23andMe, and most
telehealth-adjacent services fall outside HIPAA entirely. Dates worth citing:
GoodRx settled for $1.5M on February 1, 2023, for sharing health data for
ads; BetterHelp settled for $7.8M on March 2, 2023, for sharing
mental-health data with Facebook. In both cases, FTC Section 5 had to reach
into the gap because HIPAA didn't. Cross-reference the HIPAA-gap breakout
that runs alongside this lecture. Cold-call: name a health app on your phone;
is its data covered by HIPAA?
:::

## Breach Notification: Regulation by Consequence {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
- Before 2003 a company could be breached and tell no one. **California SB 1386** changed that; now all 50 states have a notification law
- Notification did not mandate security; it made insecurity a **headline and a board-level liability**
- You cannot outlaw breaches. You can make them impossible to hide
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
::: {.capture}
[![](images/captures/hibp.png){width="100%"}](https://haveibeenpwned.com/)

Have I Been Pwned: 1,051 breached sites, 17.9 billion addresses. Live site, captured Nov 11 2026; click to check your own.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Before 2003, a company could be breached and tell no one. California SB 1386,
effective 2003 and codified at Civil Code sections 1798.29 and 1798.82,
required notifying any California resident whose data was exposed — and
suddenly breaches were headlines. Today all 50 states plus DC, Puerto Rico,
and the Virgin Islands have breach-notification laws; the NCSL breach
tracker is the canonical map. HIPAA was amended (HITECH, 2009) to add a
similar notification duty. The teaching frame: notification didn't mandate
security; it made insecurity a PR and board-level liability. That's
"regulation by consequence" — you can't outlaw breaches, but you can make
them impossible to hide. Ask: how many students have received a breach
notice in the last year? Every hand goes up.
:::

## What a Breach Law Requires Varies {.smaller}

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 12.4
//| fig-height: 2.8
digraph breach {
  rankdir=LR; nodesep=0.25; ranksep=0.4;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=19, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.16,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=16];
bgcolor="transparent";
  b [label="Breach", fillcolor="#f8d7c4", penwidth=2];
  t [label="\"Personal information\"\nexposed?\nname + SSN, license,\naccount; some states add\nmedical, biometric, student", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  r [label="Risk-of-harm test?\nsome states: any breach;\nothers: only if harm\nis likely", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  n [label="Notify residents,\nattorney general,\ncredit bureaus;\nsome: the media", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
  d [label="Deadline:\n\"without unreasonable\ndelay\" to a fixed\nnumber of days", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
  b -> t -> r -> n -> d;
}
```

**The patchwork tax:** fifty regimes are costly, so firms apply the **strictest** state law (usually California) to everyone. California sets the national floor without Congress acting.

::: {.notes}
Fifty different regimes are genuinely costly, and the rational corporate
response is to comply with the toughest one everywhere — which is de facto one
national standard set by California, without Congress ever acting. This is the
same "California effect" that will show up in Meeting 12 when we look at
spillover from state privacy laws to national practice. Tie to the broader
theme: California has become the default U.S. privacy legislator. Debate
prompt: is that democratically legitimate — a state whose residents are
14 percent of the country setting the effective national floor — or is it the
predictable market response to a Congress that won't act?
:::

## Equifax (2017): What a Bad Response Looks Like {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **147M** Americans' data exposed
- **Six weeks** to disclose
- Stood up a separate, **spoofable** notification site
- Tried to **upsell** credit monitoring to victims

Result: **~$700M** settlement (a $575M floor); CEO resigned. The victims were never Equifax customers and could not take their business elsewhere: the FTC's **unfairness** condition in one case.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.legacy}
<!-- from ppt-archive/11-PrivacyLaw.pptx slide 29 -->
![](images/slide029_img014.png){height="215px"}

![](images/slide029_img015.png){height="190px"}
:::
::: {.caption}
CNBC, Sept 2017; the FTC's settlement summary, July 2019.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Equifax is the case study in how not to respond. Dates and numbers to say
out loud: 147M Americans exposed, disclosure delayed roughly six weeks,
notification site stood up on a domain so implausible that Krebs on Security
called the response a "dumpster fire" in September 2017, credit-monitoring
upsell to the very people whose data was leaked. Result: roughly $700M
settlement announced July 2019, including a $300M consumer-compensation fund;
CEO resigned. The data subjects were never Equifax customers — they couldn't
take their business elsewhere, which is exactly the FTC's unfairness condition
(harm not reasonably avoidable, not outweighed by benefits). Use this to
motivate why a market alone doesn't discipline data brokers, and to set up
Section 5 on the next slide.
:::


# The FTC: De Facto Privacy Regulator {.center}

No privacy statute, one very flexible section

## Section 5 of the FTC Act {.smaller}

> "**Unfair or deceptive** acts or practices in or affecting commerce are declared unlawful."

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 12.4
//| fig-height: 3.6
digraph s5 {
  rankdir=LR; nodesep=0.3; ranksep=0.5;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=18, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.18,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=16];
bgcolor="transparent";

  p [label="A company's data practice", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  q1 [label="Did it promise X\nand do Y?", shape=diamond, style="filled", fillcolor="#f2d9a8"];
  q2 [label="Substantial injury,\nnot reasonably avoidable,\nnot outweighed by benefits?", shape=diamond, style="filled", fillcolor="#f2d9a8"];
  dec [label="Deceptive\n(the easy theory: policy vs. practice)", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"];
  unf [label="Unfair\n(the hard theory: no promise needed;\nKochava, Equifax's non-customers)", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"];
  cd [label="Complaint, then a consent decree:\n20-year privacy program,\npenalties on violation", fillcolor="#d9efd3", penwidth=2];
  p -> q1; p -> q2; q1 -> dec [label="yes"]; q2 -> unf [label="yes"]; dec -> cd; unf -> cd;
}
```

A 1914 consumer-protection statute stretched into America's main privacy law: 60+ privacy cases from 2002 to 2017 and a steady stream since, with no privacy statute behind them.

::: {.notes}
The key insight to burn in: there is no federal "privacy right" being
enforced — there's a 1914 promise-keeping and anti-harm statute
(15 U.S.C. § 45) doing double duty. Deception is the easy theory — sue on
the gap between policy and practice; policy statement dates to 1983.
Unfairness is the harder theory (1980 policy statement) but reaches conduct
even when no promise was broken — that's the doctrinal move in Kochava. The
definitive academic take is Solove and Hartzog, "The FTC and the New Common
Law of Privacy," Columbia Law Review 2014 — the FTC built a common law of
privacy through 60+ cases without a privacy statute. This is improvised law,
and it's the reason a 1998 kids' law and a 1914 general statute do most of
the U.S. privacy work today.
:::

## Section 5 in Action {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Uber (2017)** — "God View" tracking of journalists, politicians, exes despite
privacy claims → consent decree + comprehensive privacy program

**Twitter (2022)** — used 2FA phone numbers for ad targeting → penalty
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Facebook (2019)** — violated its 2011 consent decree; **Cambridge Analytica**
harvested ~87M profiles → **$5B** fine, the largest ever

**Disney (2025)** — COPPA, **$10M** (see opening vignette)
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Note the mechanism: cases almost always settle with a consent decree, not a
trial — so the FTC builds privacy "common law" through orders, not statutes.
Facebook's July 2019 order is the template: $5B penalty, 20-year
comprehensive privacy program, executive certification, limits on facial
recognition and on repurposing 2FA numbers for advertising. Uber (August 2017)
was about "God View" tracking of journalists, politicians, and exes despite
privacy claims. Twitter's May 2022 $150M penalty was for using 2FA phone
numbers as an ad-targeting signal — same fact pattern the Facebook order
had already prohibited. Disney COPPA $10M closes the arc. Ask: is
governance by consent decree a feature (flexible, evolves case by case) or a
bug (no democratic input, no published rulemaking)? Good midterm question.
:::


# International: The Omnibus Model {.center}

140+ countries have privacy laws; GDPR is the gravitational center

## GDPR: Scope and Reach {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
The EU's **General Data Protection Regulation** applies to organizations:

- **located in the EU**, and
- **anywhere**, if any component is in the EU, and
- **anywhere**, if they offer goods or services to, or **monitor**, people in the EU

If EU residents can use your service, you must ask whether GDPR applies.
:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
```{dot}
//| fig-width: 6.6
//| fig-height: 4.4
digraph scope {
  rankdir=LR; nodesep=0.35; ranksep=0.5;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=18, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.16,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=16];
bgcolor="transparent";
  ex [label="A Chicago startup\nwith EU users", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"];
  a [label="Established in the EU", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; b [label="A branch, server, or\nprocessor in the EU", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; c [label="Offers goods or services to,\nor monitors, people in the EU", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"];
  s [label="In scope\n(Article 3)", fillcolor="#d9efd3", penwidth=2];
  ex -> c [style=dashed, label="e.g."]; a -> s; b -> s; c -> s;
}
```
::: {.caption}
Extraterritorial reach made GDPR the global default: the "Brussels Effect."
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Extraterritoriality is the whole game — Article 3 (territorial scope) is the
hook. A Chicago startup with EU users is in scope. Critics call it regulatory
imperialism; defenders call it the only way to protect residents in a
borderless internet. Either way, it made GDPR the global default — the
"Brussels effect," which is also the title of Anu Bradford's 2020 Oxford
University Press book. Cold-call: what U.S. law has ever had comparable
extraterritorial reach on private conduct? Very few, and none in privacy.
This is why so many U.S. state privacy laws end up copying GDPR concepts —
firms already had to build for the tougher regime.
:::

## What GDPR Requires: FIPPs With Articles {.smaller}

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 12.4
//| fig-height: 4.3
digraph map {
  rankdir=LR; nodesep=0.12; ranksep=0.9;
node [shape=box, style="filled,rounded", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=17, color="#555555", penwidth=1.4, margin="0.18,0.08"];
edge [color="#555555", penwidth=1.5, fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=15];
bgcolor="transparent";

  subgraph cluster_f { label="FIPPs (1973)"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=20; color="#bbbbbb"; style="rounded";
    f1 [label="No secret systems; know\nwhat is collected", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; f2 [label="No secondary use\nwithout consent", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; f3 [label="Access and correct\nyour record", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; f4 [label="Reasonable security", fillcolor="#cfe3f5"]; }
  subgraph cluster_g { label="GDPR (2018)"; fontname="Helvetica"; fontsize=20; color="#bbbbbb"; style="rounded";
    g1 [label="Transparency and notice\n(Art. 12–14)", fillcolor="#d9efd3"]; g2 [label="Lawful basis and purpose\nlimitation (Art. 5, 6)", fillcolor="#d9efd3"]; g3 [label="Access and rectification\n(Art. 15, 16)", fillcolor="#d9efd3"]; g4 [label="Security of processing\n(Art. 32)", fillcolor="#d9efd3"];
    n1 [label="Right to erasure\n(Art. 17)", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; n2 [label="Cross-border transfer limits\n(Art. 44–50)", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; n3 [label="Impact assessment before\nrisky processing (Art. 35)", fillcolor="#f8d7c4"]; }
  f1 -> g1; f2 -> g2; f3 -> g3; f4 -> g4;
}
```

The left column is FIPPs four decades on. The right-hand red boxes are what is new: erasure collides with the First Amendment; transfer limits have twice invalidated the EU–US arrangement (Schrems I, II).

::: {.notes}
Point out the left column is FIPPs, four decades on. The right column is what's
genuinely new and contested. Right to erasure (Article 17) comes from the 2014
Google Spain v. AEPD case — the "right to be forgotten" ruling — and collides
head-on with the U.S. First Amendment; Google delists in the EU but not the
U.S. Cross-border transfers (Chapter V, Articles 44–50): the EU has repeatedly
held the U.S. lacks "adequate" protection. Schrems I (2015) invalidated Safe
Harbor; Schrems II (2020) invalidated Privacy Shield. The EU–US Data Privacy
Framework, adopted July 2023, is the current successor and already under
legal challenge. DPIAs (Article 35) are required before risky processing.
Ask: which of these ideas would survive a U.S. First Amendment challenge if
Congress ever tried to enact them?
:::

## GDPR Enforcement Is Real {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.capture}
[![](images/captures/enforcement-tracker.png){width="100%"}](https://www.enforcementtracker.com/)

GDPR Enforcement Tracker: 3,417 fines, **€7.59B** total. Live; captured Nov 11 2026.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.capture}
[![](images/captures/dpc-tiktok.png){width="100%"}](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/latest-news/irish-data-protection-commission-fines-tiktok-eu530-million-and-orders-corrective-measures-following)

Irish DPC, May 2 2025: **TikTok €530M**, EEA-to-China transfers.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="33%"}
::: {.capture}
[![](images/captures/cnil-google.png){width="100%"}](https://www.cnil.fr/en/cookies-and-advertisements-inserted-between-emails-google-fined-325-million-euros-cnil)

CNIL, Sept 2025: **Google €325M**, ads between emails and cookie consent.
:::
:::
:::

**Meta** holds the record at **€1.2B** (2023, unlawful EU–US transfers). The 1995 Directive was omnibus on paper and famously unenforced; this is what enforcement looks like.

::: {.notes}
The numbers refute the "GDPR is toothless" claim that people made about the
old 1995 Directive (famously unenforced). Concrete anchors: TikTok €530M
(Irish DPC, May 2, 2025) — €485M under Article 46 and €45M under Article
13(1)(f), for Chinese personnel remote access; the Irish High Court stayed
the transfer-suspension order pending TikTok's appeal in September 2025.
CNIL Google €325M (September 1, 2025) — Gmail "Promotions" and "Social" tabs
contained ad emails without consent, plus a 6-clicks-to-refuse versus
2-clicks-to-accept cookie flow when creating a Google account, affecting
74 million French accounts. Meta €1.2B (May 22, 2023) — unlawful EU–US
transfers, still the all-time record. Cumulative benchmark: DLA Piper's
January 2026 survey puts total GDPR fines at €7.1B. Use the tracker live if
time allows — filter by Meta, Amazon, and Google to see the pattern.
:::

## The GDPR Debate {.smaller}

**A win for privacy — or a moat for incumbents?**

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**For**

- Real rights, real fines
- One rulebook, not 50
- Raised the global floor
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Against**

- Compliance cost favors **Big Tech**
- Cookie-consent UX fatigue
- Hasn't dented platform dominance
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a natural debate prompt (and a likely exam question) — cross-reference
the Omnibus debate that runs alongside this lecture. The strongest "against"
point: compliance cost creates a moat for incumbents who can afford CPOs
and DPIA teams; small firms can't. The strongest "for": before GDPR, the
1990s Data Protection Directive was omnibus on paper but famously unenforced,
and GDPR is what enforcement actually looks like — €7.1B says so. Ask
students to defend one side, then swap. Note that the answer often depends on
what you're optimizing for: individual redress, structural competition, or
raising the global floor.
:::


## Where U.S. Privacy Law Stands in 2026 {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.vignette}
With no federal law, the states moved: **about 20 comprehensive state privacy laws**, with Indiana, Kentucky, and Rhode Island effective **Jan. 1, 2026**. But **2025 was the first year in five with no new state law**; the wave may be leveling off.
:::

The U.S. is drifting from *purely sectoral* toward a **50-state quasi-omnibus**, without ever passing one national law.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.capture}
[![](images/captures/multistate-2026.png){width="100%"}](https://www.multistate.us/insider/2026/2/4/all-of-the-comprehensive-privacy-laws-that-take-effect-in-2026)

MultiState, Feb 4 2026. Captured Nov 11 2026; click to open.
:::
::: {.capture}
[![](images/captures/iapp-state-tracker.png){width="100%"}](https://iapp.org/resources/article/us-state-privacy-legislation-tracker/)

IAPP state privacy legislation tracker, updated Sept 2026.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the live frontier and the bridge to Meeting 12 (automated compliance
enforcement, CCPA measurement, dark patterns). Numbers to say: 20
comprehensive state laws in effect in 2026, with Indiana, Kentucky, and
Rhode Island effective January 1, 2026, and Connecticut, Arkansas, and Utah
amendments effective July 1, 2026. 2025 was the first year in five with no
new comprehensive law enacted, but 2026 is bringing a fresh wave (Alabama
passed both chambers as of April). Federal front: the American Privacy Rights
Act (APRA) expired at end of the 118th Congress in January 2025 and has not
been reintroduced — killed by fights over California preemption and the
private right of action. Only new federal privacy law of 2025 is the TAKE IT
DOWN Act (non-consensual intimate imagery plus deepfakes, 48-hour removal,
enforcement live May 2026). Texas AG's $1.375B Google settlement (October 31,
2025) is the biggest single-state privacy settlement ever. The irony to land:
the U.S. is getting something omnibus-like by accretion of state laws plus
the California-default effect — not by congressional design. Ask whether
that's a stable equilibrium.
:::

# Takeaways {.center}

- Privacy law is **reactive** — FIPPs (1973) are still the DNA
- **PII** and **notice-and-consent** are leaky models in an age of inference
- The U.S. is **sectoral** (patchwork + FTC Section 5); the EU is **omnibus** (GDPR)
- Enforcement is real and current: **Disney COPPA, TikTok €530M, CNIL Google €325M, the state wave**

::: {.notes}
Close by returning to the opening Warren and Brandeis pattern: every item
here is the law chasing a technology. Each of the three current enforcement
anchors — Disney COPPA (Dec 2025), TikTok €530M (May 2025), CNIL Google
€325M (Sept 2025) — is a law from a prior decade catching up to a technology
that outran it. FIPPs (1973) are still the DNA of everything modern.
Sectoral versus omnibus is the dichotomy to remember for the midterm. The
next meeting on automated compliance asks whether we can measure and enforce
these rules at web scale — the natural sequel to this deck. Land the plane
on the through-line: privacy law is reactive, and the reaction is speeding up.
:::
